11015-pantheism-its-story-and-significan:
J. Allanson Picton wrote this 1905 short history of pantheism for the Religions Ancient and Modern series, which aimed to present great religions, philosophies, and literary reputations to a large public. Picton argues that pantheism is not a sect or a race's religion, but a dimly discerned background to many faiths, free from limits of period or climate.

Spinoza stands as its great prophet, feeling little antagonism to any Christian sect. Picton traces forerunners in Philo, the Neo-Platonists, and Gnostics, weighing whether their views truly make the whole universe God and nothing but God. The book gives a clear, brief introduction to a difficult idea, suited to readers curious about philosophy of religion.
11768-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-i:
Printed at Oxford in 1825 as the fifth of nine volumes, this collection gathers Samuel Johnson's miscellaneous prose. Its table of contents runs from the plan and prefaces of his English dictionary to observations on Macbeth, proposals for printing Shakespeare, and a discourse to the London Chronicle.

Later pieces turn to practical questions of Johnson's day: attempts to find longitude, plans for Blackfriars Bridge, farming, the corn laws, and licensing of the stage. Together they show Johnson outside his famous dictionary and Lives, writing as a working man of letters on language, literature, trade, and public life.
12616-around-old-bethany-a-story-of-the-:
R. L. Berry's Around Old Bethany, a story of Robert and Mary Davis, first published in 1925 and long out of print, returns in a reprint edition by request. A publisher's preface explains that the true-to-life characters are led to Bible salvation. Step by step they enter Bible doctrines, and finally to a congregation of the Church of God after the New Testament pattern.

Snares of false doctrines around them are exposed, and readers are guided in truth of God's Word, armed with the sword of the Spirit to refute false teachings abroad. Berry writes evangelical narrative, plain and earnest. The book offers a Church of God conversion story, doctrinal in aim and affectionate toward its small-town saints.
13610-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
The first volume of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, published in 1927, gathers three studies: the evolution of modesty, the phenomena of sexual periodicity, and auto-erotism. Ellis, writing from years of reading and case notes, treats sex as a subject for plain scientific study rather than moral alarm.

He surveys customs of dress and shame, the monthly rhythms of the body, and solitary sexual behaviour, citing doctors and journals across Europe. Case histories sit beside theory, and Ellis argues that much long treated as vice is common human variation. The book helped move the study of sex out of the pulpit and into medicine and psychology, and it remains a landmark of early sex research.
15479-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This May 1915 number of Current History, the New York Times monthly magazine, covers the European War from April to September 1915. Its contents mix firsthand accounts, official reports, poems, and maps, giving American readers a month-by-month record while the war still raged. The issue runs from page 205, continuing the volume's sequence.

General Sir John French tells his own story of the costly victory at Neuve Chapelle. Reports cover the surrender of Przemysl to Russian siege, and the Allied fleet's disaster at the Dardanelles. Poems by Sidney Low, Marion Couthouy Smith, and Owen Seaman break the prose, and Lord Kitchener advertises for recruits. The number now reads as a wartime archive, urgent and detailed, before hindsight reshaped the story.
15510-advice-to-young-men-and-incidental:
William Cobbett published this advice in a series of letters, addressed to a youth, a bachelor, a lover, a husband, a father, a citizen, or a subject. This edition follows the 1829 text, printed at Oxford in 1906 by Henry Frowde. Cobbett speaks bluntly, as a man who has lived the life he preaches.

The first letter, to a youth of fourteen to nearly twenty, sets the book's rule. A man of hale body and sound mind has no right to live without work, unless he holds ample fortune clear of debt. Later letters treat parents, reading, history, and marriage, warning that most histories tell only battles, intrigues, and courts, with little use for present life. Cobbett's counsel is moral, practical, and combative, in the plain English that made him famous.
15830-three-years-in-europe-places-i-hav:
A travel memoir by W. Wells Brown, a fugitive slave, issued in London by Charles Gilpin in 1852, with Edinburgh sheets by Oliver and Boyd. William Farmer supplies a memoir of the author at the front. Brown spent three years in Europe, seeing places and meeting people denied him at home. His book joins travel writing to abolitionist witness.

Brown visits London, Paris, and other cities, noting manners, monuments, and the freedom of Black travellers abroad. Meetings with reformers, writers, and crowds fill the pages. His voice stays clear, proud, and observant. The memoir stands as a landmark: a formerly enslaved American telling Europe, and America, what he saw.
16488-debussy-s-pelle-as-et-me-lisande-a:
Lawrence Gilman guides listeners through Debussy's Pelleas et Melisande in this 1907 book, with musical examples from the score. He treats Debussy and his art first, then Maeterlinck's play, its action and mood, then the music itself: a revolutionary score, its themes, and how Debussy handles them. The Paris premiere of 1902 frames the discussion.

Gilman writes for opera lovers who want to hear more clearly, not for scholars alone. His prose is warm and vivid, matching the opera's dreamlike world. The book remains a fine companion for anyone meeting Pelleas for the first time, or returning to it with fresh ears.
16966-shakespearean-tragedy-lectures-on-:
A. C. Bradley, once professor of poetry at Oxford, wrote these lectures on Shakespearean tragedy, second edition, thirteenth impression, issued by Macmillan in London in 1919, first published in 1904. The lectures take up Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, and Macbeth, and Bradley dedicates the book to his students. Later impressions add formal fixes and notes on points he wished to change.

Bradley reads each hero's character as the engine of his fall, with close readings of speeches, motives, and moral shape. His lectures set the standard for 1900s Shakespeare study in English. Readers who love the great tragedies will find a rich, serious guide, best read play by play, with the plays themselves close at hand.
17093-camp-life-in-the-woods-and-the-tri:
W. Hamilton Gibson's camp manual teaches readers how to live and hunt in the woods with their own hands. Log huts, bark shanties, woodland beds, boats, and canoes come first, with notes on trappers' food and camp shelter. Then the book turns to traps of all kinds: deadfalls, gun traps, bow traps, pitfalls, and steel traps, with bait recipes for each.

Fur-bearing beasts from bear and puma down to small game each get habits, sets, and cautions, plus rules for curing and tanning skins. Gibson drew the pictures himself, and the tone is that of a skilled friend at the fire. For readers keen on old woodcraft, it remains a full, hands-on guide to a vanished outdoor trade.
19347-the-myths-of-the-new-world-a-treat:
This treatise studies the myths and symbols of the Native peoples of the Americas, from Mexico to the northern tribes. It groups stories of creation, sun and moon, heroes, and the afterlife, and asks what shared patterns of thought lie behind them. Notes cite early Spanish writers, missionaries, and government reports at length.

The author's aim is to read myth as a form of thought, not mere fancy, and to compare tribes across great distances without flattening their differences. Later scholars have revised many details, but the book remains a landmark early attempt to treat American myth as a serious subject.
19895-the-american-revolution-and-the-bo:
Sydney G. Fisher addressed an open letter to Mr. Morley on two wars. Its title pairs the American Revolution and the Boer War. A second title names its theme: the Confederacy and the Transvaal. Fisher presses Morley on when a hopeless struggle should end. A people fighting for independence, he argues, should not fight past scientific defeat. Prolonging such a war past that point becomes wrong.

Fisher was a Philadelphia historian of the Revolution. Britain's war in South Africa made Americans argue about their own past. He drew the parallel to discomfort on both sides. Open letters were the era's public dueling ground. This one is sharp, learned, and partisan. It shows historical argument doing political work.
22307-the-grammar-school-boys-of-gridley:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The Grammar School Boys of Gridley, published in 1911. Its short title names the lead boy and his friends: Dick and Co. start things moving. The scene quoted in the record is set in a classroom.

The principal calls on Master Prescott to rise and tell his story. The whole class, teacher included, is promised a good laugh. A dull, rainy day makes that laugh feel badly needed. Hancock built a long line of schoolboy books on scenes like this one. Readers get lively school life, loyal friends, and small troubles played for humor and pluck.
24330-iron-making-in-the-olden-times-as-:
The Reverend H. G. Nicholls wrote this history of iron making in the Forest of Dean, published in 1866. Its full title promises the ancient mines, forges, and furnaces of the forest, historically related on the basis of contemporary records and exact local investigation. Nicholls drew for years on the Forestal Archives of the Middle Ages and on all the information the neighborhood itself affords.

He wrote because a remarkable revival of the forest's iron works had improved the district, proving its condition depends largely on such manufacture. The book opens with the old Black Country of Gloucestershire, and the remote origin, perpetuation, and high repute of Dean iron works. Readers get a local industrial history, grounded in archives and place.
24950-bradford-s-history-of-plimoth-plan:
William Bradford's History of Plimoth Plantation, printed from the original manuscript by order of the Massachusetts General Court, records the colony's founding years in the governor's own voice. The narrative follows the settlers from persecution and exile through the Atlantic crossing to the hard first seasons at Plymouth. Letters woven through the text add the voices of sponsors, friends, and fellow planters.

The edition preserves the manuscript's inconsistent original spellings, letting readers hear the seventeenth century without modern smoothing. That roughness is part of the value: Bradford's account stays close to the events, naming shortages, disputes, and deaths alongside thanksgivings and harvests. It remains the first and fullest record of the Plymouth colony from inside.
25022-narrative-of-the-shipwreck-of-the-:
Daniel Collins's 1825 narrative, printed by John Dorr at Wiscasset, tells the shipwreck of the brig Betsey of Wiscasset, Maine. Pirates murdered five of her crew on the coast of Cuba in December 1824. Collins, one of only two survivors, takes Virgil's line for his epigraph: horrors he saw himself, and shared. The title was deposited in April 1825.

The most chilling passage finds the survivors beseeching for their lives while others pray to the mercy that saved them from the sea. Their captors sing and laugh, telling them in broken English that Americans make very good beef for their knives. Led nearly a mile from the vessel toward a cove where human bones had been seen before, with canoes hauled abreast for execution, the narrative breaks off its excerpt at horror's edge. It is a stark survivor's tale.
25064-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The June 1886 number of the New England Magazine and Bay State Monthly, old series volume four, new series volume one, leads with the Reverend N. H. Egleston on Williams College. The college, romantic in history and site amid the Berkshire hills, was born on the frontiers of civilization during the struggle to decide whether French or English would shape the continent. Its namesake, Colonel Ephraim Williams, built and commanded a line of forts along Massachusetts's northern border, from the Connecticut River to the Hoosac valley.

Williams later led a regiment toward Crown Point on Lake Champlain. He met a French force near the head of Lake George, repulsed it, and lost his life in the encounter, where alumni later raised a monument. A later piece reflects on the war's aftermath and the hard battle facing freed people on unequal terms. The number mixes institutional history with national memory.
26923-emergency-childbirth-a-reference-g:
Reprinted in December 1970 by the Office of Civil Defense and the Public Health Service, this short guide is for shelter helpers. It teaches what to do when a birth happens without a doctor. Written as Lesson 11 of a medical self-help course, it gives plain numbered rules. Stay calm, keep hands clean, let nature lead, and keep mother and baby warm and together.

The guide also lists what not to do, such as pulling on the baby or cutting the cord too soon. It walks through the stages of labor with notes on timing and care. It was made for civil defense shelters, but its calm, step-by-step tone still reads as a clear first-aid brief for childbirth.
30352-santa-fe-s-partner-being-some-memo:
Thomas A. Janvier records memorials of events in a New-Mexican track-end town in Santa Fé's Partner, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in September 1907. Janvier, author of The Passing of Thomas and The Aztec Treasure-House, tells of Palomitas in seven chapters. They run from the sage-brush hen and Hart's nephew's hold-up to Santa Fé Charley's kindergarten, Boston's lion-hunt, Shorty Smith's hanging, and the purification of Palomitas.

The narrator has ranged the Western Country, mostly years before. He has seen a little of the folks living there, and his tales carry that voice. Illustrations catch the talk and the trouble. Look by those little bushes, a notice tacked up on the depot door, and a new German kindergarten appliance. An Englishman cries that it is hotter than Sahara, and a woman groans, do not hang him, sir.
32726-death-of-a-b-e-m:
Berkeley Livingston tells a joke on science fiction itself, opening with a writer and an artist who hate bug-eyed monsters. Their publisher demands such monsters, and the pair sit in misery over coffee, sure they are setting the field back a hundred years.

Then their own tale takes over: Hiah-Leugh, chief of the Gomans on planet XYZ268PDQ, has eight eyeballs that need massaging all at once. A four-headed, six-armed slave does the work, until one eye shuts and trouble starts. Heroes Tom Brighteyes and the Leopard Girl flee the hordes of Micro Ambrosia in a wild, funny yarn.
3307-the-pagan-tribes-of-borneo-a-descri:
Charles Hose and William McDougall describe the pagan tribes of Borneo in this ethnographic work. Its full title promises an account of their physical and moral character and their customs, and the book delivers that survey from years of residence and travel in the island's interior. Longhouses, headhunting, tattoo, and rice ritual all fall within its scope.

Hose, a colonial officer, and McDougall, a psychologist, write as observers of a world already changing under colonial rule. The volume now serves as a detailed record of Borneo's peoples at the turn of the century, rich in custom and sometimes blunt in judgment. Readers of anthropology will find a classic field study, valuable for its detail and instructive in its limits.
9063-the-penance-of-magdalena-and-other-:
J. Smeaton Chase gathered these five tales from a larger work on the California missions, written with Charles F. Saunders. They center on the southern missions, south of the Tehachapi range, which Chase calls the most notable, in history and in building, of the whole chain. Each tale links a mission church to a human story.

The title tale tells of San Juan Capistrano, the greatest of the missions, raised stone by stone by Indian laborers. Other tales follow the friars and the people around them. Readers get both local lore and a sense of the old Franciscan world that still shapes how California sees its past.
advice-to-young-men-and-incidentally-to-: William Cobbett addresses young men in a series of letters that move from youth and bachelor life to lover, husband, father, and citizen. He gives blunt, practical counsel on work, money, drink, dress, and conduct, urging thrift, industry, and self-command. Though aimed at men, the letters also speak to young women, and their plain, forceful style made them a widely read conduct book.
around-old-bethany-a-story-of-the-advent: Robert Lee Berry follows Robert and Mary Davis as they search the Bible, debate in a schoolhouse, and weigh which church to join. False guides appear in Bethany, quarrels threaten, and honest confession brings good results for the pair. The story ends with a congregation formed on a New Testament pattern, as the preface urges. It is a plain religious novel meant to teach doctrine through debate and daily choice.
camp-life-in-the-woods-and-the-tricks-of:
W. Hamilton Gibson wrote a full guide to camp life and trap craft, drawn by his own hand. Shelters fill the first stock: camp roofs, log huts, and bark shanties. Wood beds and bedding sit with them. Boat and canoe builds get their own place, and camp food gets plain talk.

Trap craft fills the long heart. All the tricks and bait mixes of the trade are vowed on the title page. Steel trap use is set out step by step. Builds for traps of each kind fill a run of their own. How to take each fur beast gets full space. Skin cure and tan mixes close the craft side. Two friends, Mr. and Mrs. F. W. Gunn, who taught him in youth's bright days, get the book. Book one opens on traps for large game in the copy's first view.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antony-hickey:
Irish Franciscan theologian Antony Hickey, born in County Clare in 1586 and dead in Rome in 1641, taught and wrote abroad. Educated at home, he joined the college of St. Antony at Louvain and took the Franciscan habit in 1607. His teachers included the Irish scholars Hugh Ward and Hugh MacCaghwell, later archbishop of Armagh. After ordination he lectured in theology at Louvain and taught at St. Francis College, Cologne.

Summoned to Rome in 1619, he worked with Luke Wadding on the Franciscan annals and the works of Duns Scotus. From 1624 he lived in the college of St. Isidore. In Roman debates on the Immaculate Conception, the doctrine of Mary's sinless conception, he won distinction for learning and sharpness. Marracius called his treatise on it an outstanding and complete work. His commentary on the Sentences shows the same scholastic care.
debussy-s-pelle-as-et-me-lisande-a-guide:
A guide to Debussy's opera Pelléas et Mélisande, with music examples from the score, fills Lawrence Gilman's book. G. Schirmer of New York issued it in 1907. Gilman inscribes it to the memory of Gustave Schirmer, a lover of music of liberal taste.

Three parts treat Debussy and his art, the play and its action, and the music itself. Gilman calls the score revolutionary and traces its themes and their treatment. The opera first came out at Paris in the spring of 1902, from Maeterlinck's play. A cast list names Mary Garden as Mélisande and Jean Périer as Pelléas, with André Messager conducting. The book serves listeners who want the strange new opera made clear.
doe-osti-17152873-sam-capability-enhance:
Eric Cervi, Yang Liu, Alexandre Millischer, and Argonne colleagues teach the SAM system code to handle thermal mixing in liquid metal reactors, in report ANL/NSE-26/73. In a pool of hot liquid metal, hot and cold layers can stack instead of mixing, a pattern called stratification. During transients that layering shifts temperatures at key parts, so system codes must capture it.

Two learning models were built to predict the mixing behavior: a convolutional neural network and a transformer. Their outputs were compared against SAM's own one dimensional model. A memory saving trick compresses the transformer's attention matrix. The winning approach was then shown at system level on the ABTR reactor case, with conclusions on accuracy and cost.
doe-osti-2571716-novel-quantum-states-of:
A final technical report under grant DE-SC0023724, with Ali Yazdani of Princeton as principal investigator, sums up the 2023 Aspen Winter Conference on moiré materials. Jennifer Cano, Pablo Jarillo-Herrero, Jie Shan, and Yazdani organized the meeting, held March 12 to 17, 2023, at the Aspen Center for Physics. Moiré materials form when atom-thin sheets are stacked with a slight twist, creating patterns that reshape electron behavior.

Talks ranged across the field's open questions. They covered superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, Chern insulating phases pushed toward zero magnetic field, and Kondo physics in these systems. Other sessions presented fractional Chern insulators in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides and generalized Wigner crystals. Breaking-news sessions kept the program current. Grant funds helped early-career researchers attend, mixing theorists and experimentalists in one room for a week.
doe-osti-2587037-sam-enhancements-for-ai:
Zhiee Jhia Ooi, Gang Yang, Ling Zou, and colleagues at Argonne National Laboratory report code upgrades in ANL/NSE-25/46. The subject is SAM, the System Analysis Module, a system-level safety analysis tool for advanced reactors. The upgrades target one accident: air ingress in a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, where a break lets air into the helium coolant circuit.

Three capabilities were added. A multi-component flow model now tracks the air-helium mixture as it moves through the system. A zero-dimensional graphite oxidation model captures graphite reacting with oxygen in the incoming air, a serious concern in a graphite-moderated core. An isentropic critical flow model sharpens predictions of how fast the reactor depressurizes through a small break. Verification cases and demonstrations show each capability working, and the report also names the gaps that remain.
doe-osti-2588552-demonstration-of-a-nove:
Korbaga Woldekidan, Donald Price, Tobias Shapinsky, Maggie Sullivan, and Eric Bonnema of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this final report for ESTCP project EW22-7512, dated September 2025. Peter Curtiss, Scott Roberts, Chris Rowland, and John Gehring of S&C Electric Company share the work. It demonstrates demand management for military microgrids cut off from the main grid.

Islanded bases must balance supply and demand with limited local generation. The usual play is crude. Smart breakers shed whole buildings, but buildings with critical missions must be excluded entirely, and noncritical ones lose everything. The demonstrated alternative is automated demand response inside the fence. A microgrid controller talks to building management systems and trims equipment loads by signal. Staying on the base network also sidesteps the cybersecurity exposure of outside demand response links. In tests, the GridMaster controller held loads in sequence and survived a larger load addition before shedding became unavoidable.
doe-osti-2588595-chemical-process-safety:
Ricardo Torres leads an eight-author Pacific Northwest National Laboratory team in this assessment, dated August 2025. It was written for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research. Advanced reactors need advanced fuels. The plants that would make TRISO, metallic, and molten salt fuels handle serious chemistry. This report maps the chemical safety landscape those plants present to licensing reviewers.

For each fuel family, the team collected public information on fabrication processes. Then it worked step by step: which chemicals appear, what the physical and health safety issues are, and how severe credible accidents could be. Safeguards are covered too. One gap stands out. Exposure limits for acute releases are thin for some chemicals involved. Other limits and safety data sheets mostly close the hole. The assessment gives the regulator a foundation, while stressing that real reviews stay design-specific.
doe-osti-2589052-investigation-of-design:
David Baker of the University of Washington led this final technical report for award DE-SC0018940, on design principles for metal-binding and conductive protein assemblies. Baker's field is computational protein design: building proteins from scratch to do jobs nature never assigned. Metals give designed proteins handles for chemistry, structure, and signal.

Three objectives organize the work. The first used AI-based design to generate panels of proteins that each bind one metal ion selectively, as soluble proteins or as membrane channels. The second arrayed electronically or photonically active parts in protein fibers for nanoscale energy transport. Fibers 100 to 500 nanometers long formed and held their cargo's energy transfer potential, but proved too fragile for functional assays. The third objective pursued metal-triggered assembly: ions that switch proteins into oligomers, gate nanopores, or close nanocages and three-dimensional assemblies on command.
doe-osti-2589173-grid-modernization-of-c:
Fei Ding of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5D00-96564, dated September 2025, with Chris Bilby sharing credit. The partners were Holy Cross Energy, a Colorado cooperative, the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, and Survalent. Small co-op and municipal utilities need grid modernization too, and this project demonstrated it on a real system.

The work developed real-time data visualization and real-time distributed control of distributed energy resources, tested with Holy Cross Energy. Data flow from Survalent's SCADA, GIS, and meter systems, speaking through NRECA's MultiSpeak interoperability standard. Two to three candidate feeders at the co-op were identified for analysis. The control prize is flexibility: autonomous, distributed control of many device types can defer transmission and distribution upgrades. The project ties to a Department of Energy goal of at least 10 percent of devices actively providing grid flexibility by 2035.
doe-osti-2997298-measuring-the-interfaci:
Reading the surface chemistry of micro and nano plastics closes a laboratory project by Samantha Kruse, Mohammad Shohel, Trinity Griffus, and a large team, in Sandia report SAND2025-12205R. These tiny plastic fragments come from tire wear, burning trash, and water erosion, and they ride the air for days to weeks. People may inhale up to 70,000 such particles a day, per a study the report cites.

Existing tools could not read surface makeup with chemical detail. The team coated test particles with a matrix that lets a laser mass spectrometry method lift surface molecules for identification. Coating evenness was checked with microscope images and elemental spectra, comparing drop-cast layers against a mixed nebulization approach. A surface record matters because particles gather pollutants and oxidize as they age, changing their health effects.
doe-osti-2999879-international-nuclear-s:
Faith Carver, Travis Zipperer, Austin Hammer and co-workers at Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote these instructor guides, LA-UR-25-30161, issued 14 October 2025, for a hands-on nuclear security training kit. The kit teaches nuclear material accounting and control: the bookkeeping and seals that prove nuclear stock is where records say it is. Instructors lead classes through staged exercises with mock containers and paperwork.

Guides script each activity from setup to wrap-up. Learners handle practice apparatuses fitted with hasps and holes, envelopes, and plastic tubs standing in for material containers. They apply and remove tamper-indicating devices, seals that betray any opening, and count what remains for restocking. Notes warn that seal removal can leave residue that must be cleaned before a fresh seal goes on. Attachments describe every closure mechanism in detail. Summary sections close each exercise with key points, questions for learners, and next steps.
doe-osti-2999882-international-nuclear-s:
Faith Carver of Los Alamos assembled this instructions-for-use volume, LA-UR-25-30305, issued 17 October 2025. It serves a training kit for nuclear material accounting and control. The kit gives instructors a ready mock facility: twelve containers, pre-labelled, weighed and sealed, holding simulated material. The stand-in stock is modelled on HALEU, uranium enriched between 5 and 20 percent, under the exercise name Candium Oxide.

The volume explains how to run the exercises and how the paperwork branches. Go-to and return-to steps are marked so users never lose their place. Assumptions are stated up front: containers are metal, and seals are adhesive tamper-indicating devices. Procedures are built tough enough for a top-category facility. That depth is deliberate, to teach the full weight of real accounting controls. Added documents support graded discussions, adapting the same exercises to other materials and facility types.
doe-osti-2999885-international-nuclear-s:
Faith Carver, Travis Zipperer, Matthew Boyd and co-workers at Los Alamos National Laboratory issue this procedure set, LA-UR-25-30404, issued 20 October 2025, for a nuclear material accounting and control training kit. The procedures read as working facility documents for the kit's mock plant, so trainees practise on paperwork that feels real. Topics run from daily control duties to the reporting and resolution of accounting irregularities, any mismatch between records and material.

One core procedure assigns clear roles. Floor personnel must report a suspected irregularity at once and hold the area until it is secured. Operations management alerts the material balance custodian and orders first fixes. The custodian reports upward to the accounting manager without delay and documents every step. A revision table tracks how the set has changed with feedback from operations reviews. The documents support exercises run from the same kit, with a two-year review cycle.
doe-osti-2999886-international-nuclear-s:
Faith Carver, Travis Zipperer, Austin Hammer and co-workers at Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote these participant guides, LA-UR-25-30429, issued 21 October 2025, for a nuclear security training kit. Where instructor volumes script the teacher, these guides are the learner's own workbooks for twelve exercises in nuclear material accounting and control, the discipline that proves nuclear stock matches its records.

Exercise one sets the pattern. Participants work at a fictional facility storing nuclear material in varied containers, where management has just approved a tamper-indicating device program to cut inventory effort. Learners handle several seal types, fit each to different closing mechanisms, and judge which works best where. Later exercises build on that hands-on start. Each guide states its goals in plain numbered points and leaves room for the judgements trainees must defend, such as what an engineering analysis should weigh.
doe-osti-3001041-bi-directional-wireless:
Omer Onar of Oak Ridge and Steven Sokolsky of CALSTART close grant DE-EE-000-7799 with a final report dated 29 July 2025. The project ran from October 2016 to March 2025. The team, with Cisco, Workhorse and UPS, built wireless charging that flows both ways for medium-duty delivery trucks. A parked truck could charge without a plug, then sell power back to the grid from its battery.

The system was designed around an 11-inch ground clearance, the gap under a UPS truck, at a nominal 20 kilowatts. Coils, a three-phase grid interface and vehicle-side converters were modelled, built and tested stage by stage. They were then integrated into a Workhorse plug-in hybrid truck and demonstrated at Oak Ridge. Five operating modes for the grid-connected system were mapped. Sensitivity studies show how power transfer shifts with input and output voltage. The report assembles eight years of design and test evidence.
doe-osti-3003772-development-of-low-cost:
Mert Efe, Robin Ihnfeldt, and Aashish Rohatgi report a materials project from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, dated November 2025. It is the final account for CRADA 446, a cooperative project on low-cost magnetocaloric materials. Magnetocaloric materials heat and cool as a magnetic field cycles, which makes solid-state refrigeration possible without refrigerant gases. Cost is the barrier the project attacks.

The report follows the standard arc: objectives, experimental approach, results, and conclusions. Its reference trail points to cerium-silicon compounds, whose magnetic behavior near room temperature has drawn interest for decades. A subject invention section closes the document, as CRADA reports require. Industry partners weighing magnetic cooling for appliances or hydrogen liquefaction are the natural readers. The work tests whether cheap, abundant elements can carry the effect.
doe-osti-3006117-llnl-response-to-darpa-:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2011622, dated December 2025, is the lab's response to DARPA request for information DARPA-SN-25-94 on domestic manufacturing of emerging quantum sensors. S. Friedrich and K. Beck prepared it. The response sorts quantum sensing into classes by approach. It names atom-based devices such as clocks and interferometers, and spin-based devices such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond and atomic magnetometers. Superconducting devices such as SQUIDs form another class.

Each class sits at a different maturity level, and the response discusses lab capabilities and manufacturing challenges class by class. It backs the lab's standing with cited work, including superconducting sensor searches for sterile neutrinos and axion dark matter, and 3D-printed micro ion trap technology. The filing is a capability statement for a federal information request, not a research report, and it runs five pages plus references.
doe-osti-3006737-quality-assurance-progr:
Argonne document ANL/NE-16/17, Revision 5, is the quality assurance program plan for sodium-cooled fast reactor metallic fuel data qualification. Roberta Riel prepared the revision. The plan evaluates how the ASME NQA-1 standard applies and lays out how historical, analytical, and other data on SFR metallic fuel will be judged fit for use. Qualified data can then support future licensing efforts for advanced reactor designs.

The first data in line come from the U.S. Integral Fast Reactor program of 1984 to 1994. They include research and development data, test plans and protocols, operations and test data, and technical reports. Records of past reviews are included too, from Nuclear Regulatory Commission examinations of SFR designs. Later sections work through the quality machinery, down to software controls. System software sits under configuration change control. Every change is weighed for its impact on the product, to set the level of review and retesting required.
doe-osti-3007892-developments-to-the-dis:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2025/4107, by K. C. Goetz, Brett Witherspoon, Nick Prins, and four co-authors, dated September 2025, reports fiscal 2025 developments to the Distributed Holdup Monitoring System. Holdup is nuclear material left behind inside process equipment, and tracking it matters for both safety and accounting.

The year's work produced a first fully integrated monitor design on an 85 by 65 millimetre circuit board. A dual-core NXP microcontroller running up to 150 megahertz handles detector control, communications, data storage, power management, and the user interface. The design first leaned on power-over-ethernet networking for data collection. Smaller, integrated monitors can watch more holdup locations at once.
doe-osti-3008956-hanford-reach-fall-chin:
Hanford document HNF-72388, Revision 0, by J. J. Nugent of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions, published August 2025, reports the calendar year 2024 count of fall Chinook salmon redds in the Hanford Reach of the Columbia River. A redd is the gravel nest a salmon digs for its eggs, and the annual count tracks the spawning run.

Observers survey from aircraft flying 120 to 161 kilometres per hour near noon, when the sun angle gives the clearest view through polarized glasses. Widely spaced redds are counted one by one; tight clusters are estimated in groups of 10 or 50, with repeat passes over heavy spawning areas. The survey runs from the Interstate 182 bridge up to Priest Rapids Dam.
doe-osti-3008957-hanford-reach-fall-chin:
Hanford document HNF-72381, Revision 0, by J. J. Nugent and C. T. Lindsey of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions, published August 2025, reports the calendar year 2023 count of fall Chinook salmon redds in the Hanford Reach. It is the companion annual survey to the 2024 count, run the same way.

An aerial photography flight on November 14 caught the whole reach in clear weather, and redds showed as light patches against the darker riverbed. Analysts georeferenced the photographs and digitized each redd in a geographic information system. The total came to 7,616 redds identified across the Hanford Reach, mapped in the report's figures.
doe-osti-3011905-electrical-validation-t:
Electrical validation testing for an ORPC marine hydrokinetic generator is closed out by Calum Kenny, Scott Lambert, Ismael Mendoza, Eduard Muljadi, and Shazreen Meor-Danial of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. ORPC supplied the generator, variable frequency drives, controls, and inverter. Dynamometer testing used the Energy Systems Integration Facility and National Wind Technology Center facilities.

Simulation and parametric modelling checked power quality and grid integration for the tidal unit. A sixth modification added a feasibility study of passive direct current rectification at the turbine. Related work by an Auburn master's student showed battery storage can mitigate flicker from a tidal generator even on a weak grid.
doe-osti-3018992-multiphysics-and-multis:
Su Yan of Howard University led this final report to the National Energy Technology Laboratory, award DE-FE0032092. The project ran from September 2021 to August 2025, with the report submitted in February 2026. The goal was converting fossil fuels to hydrogen with electromagnetic energy assist. Simulation had to lead, because the physics couples across scales. Four objectives structured the work: three-dimensional structure mapping, electromagnetic hotspot mapping, multiphysics investigation, and system design with optimization. X-ray and microscopy data grounded the pore-scale structures.

Field simulations mapped where energy concentrates in the material. Thermal simulations were coupled to the field ones, so hotspots could be followed into temperature fields. Conduction current patterns in coils and workpieces changed with frequency and permeability, as the results show. The deliverable is a simulation method set, not a device. Reactor designers can now test conversion concepts in software before bending metal.
doe-osti-3030164-doe-repository-metadata:
The Energy Department Data Curation Working Group sets out a shared metadata profile in report ORNL/TM-2026/4449, from Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Olga Anna Kuchar, Abigail Martin, Brian J. Cain, and colleagues are named in the record. The department funds many repositories that hold data, papers, and software for its labs and user facilities. Each store describes its holdings its own way, which makes cross-search and machine reading hard.

The profile is a harmonization layer, not a new standard. It crosswalks six community schemas in a Rosetta-Stone style matrix, so a repository can map its fields onto the shared set without rebuilding its system. Gap ratings borrowed from the Research Data Alliance help sites judge effort. Later levels add the few missing fields needed for stronger artificial intelligence readiness.
doe-osti-3030933-unloq-understanding-coh:
Todd D. Krauss of the University of Rochester led the UNLOQ project under award DE-SC0022171, running from September 2021 to August 2025, with Pengfei Huo, A. Nickolas Vamivakas, and Michigan co-investigator Steven A. Cundiff. UNLOQ stands for Understanding Coherence in Light-Matter Interfaces for Quantum Science. The team coupled cadmium selenide nanoplatelets, flat crystals a few atoms thick, to an optical cavity. The pairing forms polaritons, half-light, half-matter states whose behavior the team mapped.

Tuning cavity loss let the group steer how the upper and lower polariton states fill. Theory work predicted a long-lived coherence, up to 200 femtoseconds at room temperature, from an effect called polaron decoupling. That coherence should show up as a beating pattern in two-dimensional electronic spectra, a signal not seen in experiments before.
doe-osti-3362876-acrrf-high-bay-dose-cal:
Jeff Cardoni, Zackary Dodson, Jesse Phillips, and Zac Jankovsky of Sandia National Laboratories compute radiation doses in report SAND2026-20690, printed May 2026. The subject is the Annular Core Research Reactor facility high bay, the tall hall above the reactor. Part B covers the worst vertical beam paths: the unshielded central cavity, the FREC-II cavity, and the neutron radiography shaft. Results feed the facility safety basis, the document that bounds how the reactor may run.

Peak dose came to about 1,430 millirem per 300 megajoule pulse, or about 40,930 rem per hour at full power on the same scale. Mesh maps show how dose falls off across the bay. One warning stands out: setting objects over the central cavity, even a thin steel plate, can make the scattered field above it significantly worse.
doe-osti-3364003-laser-spectroscopy-of-e:
A final report to the DOE Office of Science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology closes award DE-SC0021179. The Early Career Research Program project was led by Ronald Fernando Garcia Ruiz from September 2020 to September 2025. The project used laser spectroscopy, shining tuned laser light on atoms to read their structure, to study exotic atoms and molecules built around actinide isotopes. These short-lived radioactive nuclei are predicted to be pear-shaped, a rare deformation called octupole deformation.

Pear-shaped nuclei amplify signals that would reveal new physics, such as violations of fundamental symmetries. The team produced and measured these fragile systems despite their scarcity and short lifetimes. Results map nuclear, atomic, and molecular structure across the isotopes studied. The work supports precision searches planned at current and future radioactive beam facilities.
doe-osti-3365512-development-of-composit:
University of California, Irvine's final report for DOE award DE-EE0008838, led by Shane Ardo with eight partner institutions, covers October 2019 to October 2023 work on photocatalysts that split water with sunlight. The target: particle suspensions that turn at least 10 percent of solar energy into hydrogen, the efficiency a practical dual-bed reactor needs to hit DOE cost goals. Perovskite oxide particles were the platform.

Strategies attacked the materials' light absorption and charge handling. Single-particle studies of rhodium-doped strontium titanate found a trap state 0.34 electron volts below the conduction band, matching the roughly 2.8 electron volt optical transition seen in luminescence. Heat-dependent transport tests on single nanoparticles tied the traps to oxygen vacancies. Partners from Columbia to Tokyo universities contributed reactor designs in the Z-scheme arrangement, where two photocatalysts split the water-splitting job.
doe-osti-3366323-macroalgae-cultivation-:
A technical progress report for ARPA-E award DE-AR0000920 covers the MACMODS macroalgae modeling project at the University of California, Irvine, led by Kristen Davis, from May 2018 to June 2024. MACMODS predicts how ocean seaweed farms grow and interact with currents, so farms can be sited and designed on evidence. The project was transferring to Stanford as the PI moved institutions.

Field observations ran at three farms, reaching 82 percent completion for that milestone, including the 86-acre Ocean Rainforest site offshore Santa Barbara in summer 2024. Model validation against farm growth data reached 95 percent. Published work shows kelp farms generating their own Langmuir circulations and pulling nutrients upward by turbulent mixing. A model-informed farm design paper appeared in June 2024.
doe-osti-3375395-proliferated-resilient-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2019863, by John Cortes Gutierrez and dated June 2026, presents PREEMPT, a concept for swarms of small space telescopes. The name spells out Proliferated Resilient Economical Half-Meter Aperture Space Telescopes. Today's imaging payloads for spy and space-watch work can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. PREEMPT bets that many cheap half-meter scopes can do the same work. The project ran as an LDRD effort coded 23-ERD-052.

The team sorted its current monolithic optic against the new plan. It then drafted the V20 payload, a fifty-centimeter scope, as the next step. Runs of structural, shake, and heat tests flagged the main risks. The design looks workable, with heat control as the chief worry. Side work built a nonlinear model of Viton, the seal material at the optic mount, and showed printed metal composites can serve in a payload.
doe-osti-3387426-fast-1-2-2-a-computer-c:
FAST-1.2.2: A Computer Code for Thermal-Mechanical Nuclear Fuel Analysis under Steady-State and Transients, dated May 2026, is the manual for the FAST code. It was prepared for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research. Six Pacific Northwest authors are printed, led by K. J. Geelhood, with J. Corson and J. J. Whitman of the commission. The code was developed under the NQA-1-2017 quality standard.

FAST computes how a fuel rod behaves in a running reactor. It tracks heat conduction through the pellet, mechanical strain, and coolant heating, in steady operation and transients. It uses a single-channel coolant enthalpy rise model. It uses a finite difference heat conduction model with mesh spacing finer at the pellet edge, where high-burnup fuel peaks in power. This volume covers structure, limits, model summaries, and input instructions. Companion volumes assess predictions against measured fuel data and document the MatLib models.
doe-osti-3409099-mechanical-electrochemi: Crash-testing an EV battery is expensive — simulating it is cheaper, if the model is right. Santhanagopalan and Lim's final report builds mechanical, electrochemical, and thermal models of EV batteries for crash simulation. The combined models predict how a battery bends, heats, and fails when metal meets metal.
doe-osti-3409100-mechanical-electrochemi:
Report NLR/TP-5700-100722 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, covers training on linked mechanical, electrical, and thermal battery models. Anudeep Mallarapu was the lab contact, with Jaeyoung Lim in the evidence record. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-19-00798.

One study used strain as the trigger for internal short circuit in a high-capacity cell. Voltage dropped sharply when that rule fired in the model. The team built and checked a combined model of the short inside a finite element tool. Trainees learn how a crush fault can turn into heat and failure inside a vehicle battery.
doe-osti-3626701-hanford-reach-fall-chin:
Hanford report HNF-73706, Revision 0, published in August 2026, tracks fall Chinook salmon spawning nests in the Hanford Reach for calendar year 2025. J. J. Nugent, C. T. Lindsey, and M. F. Paulsen of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions wrote it for the DOE Hanford Field Office. A redd is the gravel nest a salmon digs to lay eggs. Counting redds shows returning fish numbers.

Crews surveyed the reach from the air and digitized each redd they could see. Maps divide the river into upper, middle, and lower parts and plot redd density for 2025. Charts place the year in counts back to 1948 and link peak counts to estimated escapement from 1964 onward. Visibility had limits: nests in deep water or in thick clusters low in the reach were hard to see. Redds showed in water up to seven metres deep.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DrenasWilliamM_:
Officer J. D. Tippit was murdered in Dallas shortly after President Kennedy was shot, and his killing became a second crime at the center of that day. Bi Drenas built a research study of the Tippit murder titled Car #10, Where Are You? The study rests on the witnesses' own words.

Drenas questions the official investigation rather than repeating it. By working from testimony, the study lets each witness's account stand against the version the public was given. For readers of the Dallas evidence, it is a close, skeptical reading of the case that is often treated as settled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GildayWilliamM_: Nsia-GildayWilliamM Gilday William M: the made public government document, captured as titled, subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued, an obscure item, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingMartinLuthe:
Playbill, the theater program magazine, marked its fifteenth anniversary with an issue honoring Martin Luther King Jr. The issue features King's final published statement, A Testament of Hope. It also carries a feature called The Decent Society, taking its theme from King's own hopes for the country.

A theater magazine honoring a preacher shows how wide King's place in American culture had become. His last published words reached readers between the covers of a Broadway program book. The issue preserves that tribute whole, King's testament printed by an industry far from his pulpit.

On July 17, 1968, the Memphis Police Department's Inspectional Bureau issued a report on its security and surveillance of Martin Luther King Jr. Assistant Chief W. E. Routt wrote it. The report covers the period from King's arrival in Memphis on April 3 until his assassination there.

King had come to Memphis to support striking sanitation workers. The report records how the department watched and guarded him during those final days. As an internal police account written three months after the murder, it shows what the department said its own role had been. It also preserves the names, posts, and routines of the officers assigned to him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MoranElizabethM: Elizabeth Moran: the garbled letter apparently addressed to 'Weisberg' - the substance is not recoverable. Damaged, but kept, complete. A single letter, filed. An obscure item. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RequestForMoney: Harold Weisberg wrote this letter to a member of the House of Representatives. It concerns the House Select Committee on Assassinations, which was then reinvestigating the King and Kennedy murders. The file's own label ties it to a request made in 1978. Weisberg's letters to Congress usually asked for records, oversight, or help with agencies. The file does not name the member or summarize this letter, so its specific request cannot be stated.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TurnerFayM_Turn: Fay M. Turner testified before the Warren Commission about what he heard on the day of the Kennedy assassination. Questioned by commission lawyer Mr. Belin, he gave his account under oath. The commission questioned hundreds of witnesses this way in 1964. Turner's testimony is one voice in that large record, preserved so readers can weigh what bystanders said they saw and heard in Dallas.
govdocs-archive_org-the-viking-king-of-p: Jacques de Mahieu claimed that Vikings reached South America long before Columbus. The Viking King of Paraguay tells his account of alleged Norse settlement in Paraguay. Mainstream historians reject such claims for lack of evidence. The library holds the book as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe history. It serves the study of diffusionist theories: bold stories about ancient voyages that evidence has not confirmed.
nasa-tm-19640018170-effect-of-compressib:
M. P. Singh of Goddard Space Flight Center's theoretical division wrote this paper. It studies drag on a ball that vibrates in a special fluid. The fluid conducts electricity, is thick, and can be compressed. Rotation and a magnetic field act on the flow as well.

Singh's introduction ties the math to motions inside Earth itself. Flow in Earth's liquid core may make the planet's magnetic field, he notes. Spinning forces and magnetic forces there interact in complex ways. The near match of geographic and magnetic poles hints at spin's strong role. His vibrating ball is a clean model for forces that also shape planets and stars.
nasa-tm-19650014109-coriolis-effects-dur:
John D Stewart and Brant Clark studied a subtle effect on pilots inside a moving flight simulator. When the cab pitches or rolls, extra forces act on the balance organs in the inner ear. Those forces can make a pilot feel motion that is not really happening. The study used the Ames five-degree-of-freedom simulator.

Three modes of simulator motion were tested. The authors looked at strong Coriolis effects and at false feelings of position in space. Such illusions matter, because a pilot who misreads motion may react wrongly. Knowing where the illusion starts helps designers keep simulator training honest and safe.
nasa-tm-19680011015-photomeson-productio:
F. W. Stecker, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, reopens a cosmic ray question in February 1968. Very energetic cosmic rays should lose energy by making mesons when they strike the universe's microwave glow. Many expected the cosmic ray spectrum to fall off sharply at the top for that reason.

Stecker reexamines that photomeson effect on the high-energy spectrum. His reexamination leads to a softer conclusion. The spectrum, he finds, may not steepen abruptly at high energy after all. The result mattered for how far the most energetic cosmic rays can travel before the microwave background robs their energy.
nasa-tm-19690028198-summary-of-particle-: James I. Vette of Goddard Space Flight Center sums up particle groups in the magnetosphere in this September 1969 preprint, numbered X-614-69-313. Trapped electrons and protons fill the zone around Earth in belts. Those belts can harm spacecraft and crews. The report record describes the mean behavior of those groups over time. A summary like this gives planners base levels for radiation risk. The hosted sample holds the cover page only, after a modern copy notice. No group values can be stated from the sample.
nasa-tm-19700026567-vacuum-deposition-of:
Vacuum deposition of semiconductor materials is the subject of this report from the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. The materials belong to the 3-5 family, named for the columns of their elements. The work uses the three-temperature deposition method to lay them down as films for thin film transistor work.

The work grew out of a summer faculty fellowship program and centers on indium antimonide films. Indium and antimony were laid down together in vacuum to form the compound film. Measured mobility in those films ran well above the values of films then in common use. The authors detail their procedures, note the gain over cadmium selenide films, and recommend directions for future work.
nasa-tm-19720017873-mechanical-propertie:
William D Klopp and Walter R Witzke of the Lewis Research Center reported these alloy tests in June 1972, as NASA TM X-2576. They studied molybdenum melted by electron beam, plus three dilute molybdenum rhenium alloys. Pure molybdenum turns brittle at low temperatures, which limits its use. Small rhenium additions were known to help tungsten greatly. The study asked whether the same trick worked for molybdenum, and measured the strength effects.

All three alloys stayed ductile to colder temperatures than the pure metal. The richest alloy improved the changeover point by about two hundred degrees Celsius. Rhenium also raised tensile strength at low and high heat. High temperature creep strength rose as well. The pattern matched what dilute tungsten rhenium alloys had shown earlier.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
May 1915 forms number two of volume two in the New York Times Current History of the European War. The magazine ran from April to September 1915, with an index. General Sir John French tells his own story in this number, with a map.

French's account centres on the costly victory of Neuve Chapelle. Sidney Low's poem Roberts of Kandahar follows the general's report. Another long piece tells how Przemysl, Galicia's strong fortress, yielded to a Russian siege, with maps. A poem called The Jesters lightens the run of battle reports. The number mixes commanders' words, verse, and siege news for American readers at home.
pantheism-its-story-and-significance-rel: J. Allanson Picton's Pantheism: Its Story and Significance belongs to a popular series. The series is Religions Ancient and Modern. Each small volume cost one shilling net. The hosted sample shows the series advertisement only. Jane Harrison's Religion of Ancient Greece appears in it. Edward Clodd's Animism and H. A. Giles's Religions of Ancient China appear too. Volumes on Islam, Buddhism, and Hinduism were in preparation. No page of Picton's own argument appears in the sample.
podcast-dannyjones--y7DDPR2L-M:
Steve-O built his fame on Jackass, performing stunts that repeatedly put his body, and sometimes his life, at risk. Sitting with Danny Jones, he talks about the other side of that life: God, near-death experiences, and his own cheerful conviction that he is probably going to hell.

The tone swings between confession and comedy, which suits a guest whose career mixed both. Steve-O reflects on survival, addiction and recovery form the background of his story, and faith arrived late in it. Jones gives him room to be serious without sanding off the humor. The episode works as a celebrity interview with real weight, because the man describing brushes with death has had more of them than almost any guest on the show.
podcast-joerogan-t8h3-c-sJ-M:
Amanda Feilding, the British researcher who founded the Beckley Foundation, talks psychedelics and the ego in this Joe Rogan Experience segment. Feilding spent decades funding careful science on drugs that most labs avoided. Her foundation backed studies on LSD, cannabis, and consciousness itself.

Feilding explains how psychedelics can loosen the ego, the tight sense of self that runs daily life. She connects that effect to possible help for depression and addiction. Rogan asks about her own long, unusual path in science and policy. The segment gives drug research a patient, scholarly voice rarely heard on the show.
podcast-tuckercarlson-PpF26prP0_M:
Country star Jason Aldean joins Tucker Carlson for a heartfelt talk about fame and fire. Aldean was on stage during the Las Vegas mass shooting. That night still shapes his life and music.

He tells what he saw and how he coped after the attack. The title also names school policy on gender and fights inside country music. Aldean defends his small-town anthem and the backlash it drew. Carlson draws out a star who refuses to bend. The episode suits country fans who want the man behind the songs, unfiltered.
rogozhin-diela-moskovskoi-tsenzury-v-tsa: Diela Moskovskoi tsenzury v tsarstvovanie Pavla I, by Rogozhin. The Moscow censorship. This book preserves that study. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
shakespearean-tragedy-lectures-on-hamlet:
A. C. Bradley, formerly professor of poetry at Oxford, published these lectures on four great tragedies with Macmillan. A first edition came in 1904; this second edition of 1919 marks the thirteenth impression. Bradley treats Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, and Macbeth in turn.

Lecture by lecture, Bradley traces character, plot, and the moral world each play builds. His readings set the terms for a century of talk on Shakespearean tragedy. Students still meet Hamlet's delay and Lear's storm through Bradley's lens, even when they argue with it, since few critics have matched his care or his reach.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume I of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, in the 1927 printing, holds three studies: The Evolution of Modesty, The Phenomena of Sexual Periodicity, and Auto-Erotism. Ellis's general preface traces the work to his youth, spent partly in an Australian city and partly in the solitude of the bush.

There, he says, a resolve grew in him that a main part of his life's work should be to make the problems of sex clear. An earlier book, Man and Woman, served as his introduction to the ground. The studies that follow treat shame, rhythm, and self-love as natural facts to be mapped with care rather than as sins to be hushed.
the-myths-of-the-new-world-a-treatise-on:
Daniel G. Brinton's The Myths of the New World was published in 1868. Leypoldt and Holt issued it in New York, and Trubner and Company in London. Only a transcriber's note and title page are present here, so the treatise itself does not appear. The subtitle describes a treatise on the symbolism and mythology of the Red Race of America, the period's term for Native American peoples.

Brinton's credentials fill the title page: degrees, membership in the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Philadelphia, and corresponding membership in the American Ethnological Society. His Notes on the Floridian Peninsula is named as an earlier work. The transcriber's note explains markings for preserved misprints and Greek-letter passages.
the-pagan-tribes-of-borneo-a-description: Only an old-style Project Gutenberg header is present here for The Pagan Tribes of Borneo, by Hose and McDougall. The header line names the book and its two authors, and the rest is standard notice about copyright laws, donations, and keeping the file intact. No title page, contents, or chapter text appears among the pages present. The book's own account of the peoples of Borneo therefore cannot be described from them; title and authors are all they supply.
the-penance-of-magdalena-and-other-tales:
J. Smeaton Chase wrote The Penance of Magdalena and other tales of the California missions. His foreword says the tales were drawn from The California Padres and Their Missions, written with Charles F. Saunders. The southern missions, he notes, form a natural unit south of the Tehachapi, and five of the most notable are included here.

The first tale opens at San Juan Capistrano. Slowly the great mission rose among the hills, built brick by brick by Indian laborers under the Fathers. Timbers of pine and sycamore came by ox team from Palomar, the Mountain of Doves. Among the workers was a boy christened Lucas, renamed Te-filo by Padre Josef for his excellence. Chase mixes mission history with story.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-in-nine: Volume five of Johnson's works, in the nine-volume 1825 Oxford English Classics printing, appears as a contents list of miscellaneous pieces. The plan and preface of his English dictionary lead the volume. His observations on Macbeth follow. Proposals for printing Shakespeare's works are included. Pieces on Milton, longitude, and Blackfriars Bridge also appear. The essays themselves do not follow in the opening pages provided.
three-years-in-europe-places-i-have-seen: W. Wells Brown, described on his title page as a fugitive slave, wrote Three Years in Europe, published at London and Edinburgh in 1852. William Farmer supplied a memoir of the author. Brown's subtitle promises places seen and people met. Contents show letters beginning with departure from Boston, the passage, first sight of land, and Liverpool. A second letter travels to Ireland and Dublin during a royal visit, visiting Thomas Moore's birthplace. The opening contents are what is given in this record, so Brown's letters themselves do not appear.
